## What can go wrong

`inla_vanilla()` approximates a posterior in stages, and each stage can fail
in its own way. The mode search can stop short. The Gaussian can be a poor
centre, so the VB correction moves far. A skew-normal can fail to match the
shape of a marginal. And each marginal is fitted to a scan of only
$\pm 4$ posterior SDs around the mode, so whatever lies beyond is
extrapolated. A posterior SD in these checks is the Laplace SD at the mode,
$\sqrt{\Sigma_{jj}}$, as in INLAvaan; it is not the SD column of the summary
table, which is the skew-normal's.

Each stage is checked as it runs, at almost no cost: the checks reuse what the
fit has already computed. `summary()` reports every check and flags the
values that look off, and `diagnostics()` returns them as numbers. Most
problems also raise one warning at the end of the fit. Printing the fit ends
with a line counting its warnings and one counting the flagged checks, each
shown only when there are any, so even a fit run with `silent = TRUE` shows
that something needs a look.

| Check | In `diagnostics(fit, type = "param")` | Flagged by `summary()` | Fit-time warning | From |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mode | `mode_shift_sigma` | above 0.1 SDs | the same | INLAvaan |
| Hessian | `hess_cond` (in `diagnostics(fit)`) | above $10^8$ | the same | INLAvaan |
| VB correction | `vb_shift_sigma` | above 1 SD | the same | INLAvaan |
| Skew-normal fit | `nmad` | above 0.1 | the same | INLAvaan |
| Scan-end mass | `scan_end_mass` | above 0.05 | the same | INLAvaan |
| Tails | `tails` | heavy | the same | inlavanilla |
| Scan path | `bend` | above 0.1 nats | no | inlavanilla |
| Skew-normal and VB means | `sn_vs_vb` | above 0.1 SDs | no | inlavanilla |

Most of these are the checks of INLAvaan's `diagnostics()`, under the same
names. Jamil and Rue (2026) use the VB shift and NMAD as fit diagnostics,
and the gap between the skew-normal and VB means as an internal check; the
mode shift, the Hessian condition number and the scan-end mass come from
INLAvaan's `diagnostics()`, not from the paper. The levels of those five
checks are INLAvaan's, and the fit-time warning uses its words. The tails
check is inlavanilla's own, and so are the scan-path and SN-VB checks, which
only `summary()` flags. Every level is a package default, chosen so that a
healthy fit stays silent, and not a calibrated cut-off: a tripped check is a
prompt to look again, and silence is not a certificate of accuracy. In the
simulations of Jamil and Rue (2026, Section 4.4), the VB shift and NMAD track
the loss of accuracy, and the paper reports a calibration of the expected
error against them in its Supplementary Material.

## A healthy fit

Poisson counts with a Gamma(2, 1) prior on the rate, on the log scale:

```{r}
#| label: healthy
library(inlavanilla)

y <- c(2, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 1)
logpost_pois <- function(theta, y) {
  rate <- exp(theta[["log_rate"]])
  sum(dpois(y, rate, log = TRUE)) +
    dgamma(rate, 2, 1, log = TRUE) +
    theta[["log_rate"]] # the Jacobian
}
fit_pois <- inla_vanilla(logpost_pois, c(log_rate = 0), y = y, silent = TRUE)
summary(fit_pois)
```

Every check passes. The marginal is mildly skewed (shape about -1.4), the
skew-normal matches the scan to within 1% of its peak (NMAD), and its mean
agrees with the VB-corrected mean.

## The mode, the Hessian and the VB correction

The mode is checked by the Newton step there, in posterior SDs
(`mode_shift_sigma`): how far one step of Newton's method would still move
each parameter. It is flagged above 0.1, INLAvaan's level, whatever the
optimiser's return code, because without a gradient the optimiser can report
failure at an accurate mode, and success short of one. When the mode is off,
the warning says so first, and suggests what to change.

`hess_cond` is the condition number of the Hessian at the mode, with each
parameter in posterior-SD units: the ratio of the largest to the smallest
eigenvalue of the posterior correlation matrix. Above $10^8$ some
combination of the parameters is weakly identified. INLAvaan takes the
condition number on the raw scale of the parameters, where a mere change of
units can make it large; inlavanilla allows posterior SDs from $10^{-6}$ to
$10^4$, so it measures it in posterior SDs instead.

The VB correction recentres the Gaussian at the shift that minimises its
Kullback-Leibler divergence from the posterior (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Section
3.1). `vb_shift_sigma` is how far it moved each mean from the mode, in
posterior SDs (`vb_shift` is the same shift on the scale of `logpost`, and
`kld`, half its square, the Kullback-Leibler divergence of each shifted
marginal). A shift of a few tenths is normal for a skewed posterior; a shift
above 1 SD means that the posterior is far from the Laplace Gaussian. When
the fixed-point iteration hands over to the optimiser, `fit$diagnostics$vb`
records it, and `summary()` and the verbose output report it, but, as in
INLAvaan, it is not flagged: it is a route of the solver, not a sign of a
poor approximation.

The skew-normal mean and the VB mean both estimate the posterior mean, by
different routes, so they should agree closely (Jamil & Rue, 2026,
Proposition 3.4); a gap signals higher-order effects or numerical error
(Section 5.1). `sn_vs_vb` is their gap in posterior SDs, and a gap above 0.1
is flagged.

## The skew-normal fit

`nmad` is the largest gap between the fitted skew-normal and the scanned
log-posterior, on the density scale and relative to the peak (Jamil & Rue,
2026, Section 4.4). A skew-normal has one mode and one direction of skew, so
it cannot follow a marginal with two bumps:

```{r}
#| label: mixture
logpost_mix <- function(theta) {
  log(0.7 * dnorm(theta[[1]], 0, 1) + 0.3 * dnorm(theta[[1]], 3, 1))
}
fit_mix <- inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2))
```

The fit ends with one warning that lists every problem. The second bump puts
mass far beyond what the Laplace SD expects, so the skew-normal fits the scan
poorly, it stretches its own tail out of the scanned window to cover the
bump, and the tails are heavy. `diagnostics()` gives the numbers behind the
warning, for the whole fit and for each parameter:

```{r}
#| label: mixture-diagnostics
diagnostics(fit_mix)
diagnostics(fit_mix, type = "param")
```

`plot(type = "sn_fit")` shows the fit against the scan it was fitted to, as
INLAvaan's plot of the same name does: on the scan coordinate, in posterior
SDs from the mode, the log-posterior along the scan ("Raw"), the same with
the volume correction added ("Corrected"), and the fitted skew-normal. NMAD
is the largest gap between the last two. `type = "sn_fit_log"` draws the same
on a log scale.

```{r}
#| label: mixture-sn-fit
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "The scanned log-posterior of the mixture, as a density scaled to a peak of 1, with its second bump to the right, and the fitted skew-normal, a single skewed bump that runs below the main peak and above the dip between the two."
plot(fit_mix, type = "sn_fit")
```

Against the exact density, the skew-normal covers both modes but follows
neither:

```{r}
#| label: mixture-plot
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-alt: "The fitted skew-normal against the exact bimodal density. The skew-normal is a single skewed bump that covers both modes of the exact density but follows neither."
# The skew-normal density, from the fit's xi, omega and alpha
dskewnorm <- function(x, xi, omega, alpha) {
  z <- (x - xi) / omega
  2 / omega * dnorm(z) * pnorm(alpha * z)
}
theta <- seq(-4, 7, length.out = 400)
exact <- 0.7 * dnorm(theta, 0, 1) + 0.3 * dnorm(theta, 3, 1)
sn <- fit_mix$sn[1, ]
fitted <- dskewnorm(theta, sn[["xi"]], sn[["omega"]], sn[["alpha"]])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(
  theta, exact, type = "l", lwd = 2, las = 1, bty = "n",
  xlab = "theta", ylab = "density", ylim = c(0, 0.33)
)
lines(theta, fitted, col = "#eb6834", lwd = 2)
legend(
  "topright", c("exact", "skew-normal fit"),
  col = c("black", "#eb6834"), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
)
```

## The scan path

Each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, the path
on which the Laplace Gaussian puts the other parameters at their conditional
mode given this one (Jamil & Rue, 2026, Lemma 3.1). The straight line is a
first-order approximation to a possibly curved ridge (Section 3.2.1). When
the true conditional mode bends away from the line, the scan misses
log-density, and the marginal comes out too narrow. `bend`, inlavanilla's
own check, is the log-density, in nats, that one Newton step in the other
parameters would recover at $\pm 2$ posterior SDs.

This happens when a parameter's spread depends on another parameter that the
data pin down poorly. A normal mean with an unknown SD, from 12
observations, is the textbook case:

```{r}
#| label: bend
set.seed(4)
y12 <- rnorm(12, 10, 2)
logpost_norm <- function(theta, y) {
  sum(dnorm(y, theta[["mu"]], exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]), log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(theta[["mu"]], 0, 100, log = TRUE) +
    dnorm(theta[["log_sigma"]], 0, 10, log = TRUE)
}
fit_norm <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost_norm, c(mu = 9, log_sigma = 0.5), y = y12, silent = TRUE
)
signif(fit_norm$diagnostics$marginals[, c("nmad", "bend")], 2)
```

`summary()` flags the bend for `mu`. The exact marginal SD of `mu`, from a
grid, shows how much narrower the skew-normal is:

```{r}
#| label: bend-exact
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(7, 15, length.out = 401),
  log_sigma = seq(-1, 2.5, length.out = 401)
)
lp <- apply(grid, 1, function(g) logpost_norm(g, y12))
w <- exp(lp - max(lp))
w <- w / sum(w)
m <- sum(w * grid$mu)
sds <- c(exact = sqrt(sum(w * (grid$mu - m)^2)), skew_normal = fit_norm$summary["mu", "SD"])
sds
```

The skew-normal SD of `mu` is `r round(100 * (1 - sds[[2]] / sds[[1]]))`% too
small here. The gap shrinks as $1/n$: for a normal mean with an unknown SD it
is about 3% at 50 observations and under 1% at 200. The `bend` value says
which parameters are at risk, not exactly how much.

## Tails and scan-end mass

Both checks are about the edge of the scanned window, but they look at
different things:

* `tails` reads the **log-posterior itself** at the two ends of the scan. It
  is flagged when either end is still within 3 nats of the peak, that is, when
  the density there is over 5% of its peak. A Gaussian is 8 nats down at
  $\pm 4$ SDs.
* `scan_end_mass` is the mass the **fitted skew-normal** puts beyond the
  window, where it is extrapolated (as INLAvaan's `diagnostics()` reports
  it). A Gaussian marginal gives $2\Phi(-4) = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}$; the
  larger it is, the more of the marginal is extrapolated.

Neither one can see the mass the true posterior has beyond the window. The
figure shows three one-parameter posteriors whose exact densities are known.
The x axis is in posterior SDs from the mode, so the scanned window is always
$-4$ to $4$ (the grey band).

```{r}
#| label: tails-cases
#| include: false
# Each case: the fit, and the exact log-posterior (up to a constant)
case <- function(logpost, init, zlim, ...) {
  fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init, ..., silent = TRUE)
  mode <- fit$mode[[1]]
  sd <- sqrt(fit$cov[1, 1])
  lp_theta <- function(t) logpost(stats::setNames(t, names(init)), ...)
  lp_z <- function(z) vapply(mode + z * sd, lp_theta, 0)
  # The exact mass outside the window, integrated over the whole line
  dens <- function(t) {
    d <- exp(vapply(t, lp_theta, 0) - lp_theta(mode))
    d[!is.finite(d)] <- 0 # far out, where the log density overflows
    d
  }
  total <- integrate(dens, -Inf, Inf, rel.tol = 1e-8)$value
  outside <- (integrate(dens, -Inf, mode - 4 * sd, rel.tol = 1e-8)$value +
    integrate(dens, mode + 4 * sd, Inf, rel.tol = 1e-8)$value) / total
  z <- seq(zlim[1], zlim[2], length.out = 3000)
  dz <- diff(z)[1]
  ref <- lp_z(z)
  ref_d <- exp(ref - max(ref))
  ref_d <- ref_d / sum(ref_d * dz)
  sn <- fit$sn[1, ]
  # the fitted skew-normal density, on the z scale
  u <- (mode + z * sd - sn[["xi"]]) / sn[["omega"]]
  sn_d <- sd * 2 / sn[["omega"]] * dnorm(u) * pnorm(sn[["alpha"]] * u)
  zs <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 21)
  scan <- lp_z(zs) - lp_z(0)
  d <- fit$diagnostics$marginals
  list(
    z = z, ref_d = ref_d, sn_d = sn_d, zs = zs, scan = scan,
    tails = d$tails, sem = d$scan_end_mass, ref_out = outside
  )
}
# A variance that the data can only bound from above: y ~ N(0, 1 + v), with
# a Gamma(1, 0.5) prior on sqrt(v), on the log scale
z100 <- qnorm(ppoints(100))
y_var <- z100 / sqrt(mean(z100^2)) * sqrt(1.5)
logpost_var <- function(theta, y) {
  v <- exp(theta[[1]])
  sum(dnorm(y, 0, sqrt(1 + v), log = TRUE)) +
    dgamma(sqrt(v), 1, 0.5, log = TRUE) + log(sqrt(v) / 2)
}
cases <- list(
  case(logpost_pois, c(log_rate = 0), zlim = c(-8, 8), y = y),
  case(function(theta) dt(theta[[1]], 1, log = TRUE), c(theta = 0.1), zlim = c(-14, 14)),
  case(logpost_var, c(log_v = -0.7), zlim = c(-14, 8), y = y_var)
)
titles <- c("Well behaved", "Heavy inside the window", "Heavy beyond the window")
subs <- c("Poisson log rate", "a Cauchy posterior", "a variance near zero")
```

```{r}
#| label: tails-figure
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| dpi: 144
#| fig-alt: "Three columns, one posterior each. Top row: the log density with the scan points, the ends of the scan and a line 3 nats below the peak. Bottom row: the density, with the mass outside the scanned window shaded for the exact posterior and for the skew-normal fit. In the first column both are tiny. In the second the scan ends sit above the 3-nat line, so tails is flagged, and the exact posterior has much more mass outside the window than the fit. In the third the scan ends are just below the line, and the exact posterior again has more mass outside than the fit."
ink <- "#0b0b0b"
ink2 <- "#52514e"
muted <- "#8a8984"
grid_col <- "#e4e3df"
col_sn <- "#eb6834"
col_lap <- "#2a78d6"
band <- "#efeeea"
fade <- function(col, a) grDevices::adjustcolor(col, a)
fmt <- function(x) {
  if (x < 1e-3) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1) else formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
}

op <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
layout(rbind(c(1, 1, 1), c(2, 3, 4), c(5, 6, 7)), heights = c(0.10, 0.47, 0.43))
par(cex = 0.85)
par(mar = c(0, 1, 0.5, 1))
plot.new()
legend(
  "center", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.95, text.col = ink,
  text.width = c(0.14, 0.14, 0.09, 0.11, 0.1),
  legend = c("exact posterior", "skew-normal fit", "Laplace", "scan points", "scan ends"),
  col = c(ink, col_sn, col_lap, muted, ink), lty = c(1, 1, 2, NA, NA),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 1.6, NA, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, NA, 16, 21),
  pt.bg = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, "white"), pt.cex = c(NA, NA, NA, 0.9, 1.4)
)
for (k in 1:3) {
  cs <- cases[[k]]
  par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 3.4, 0.8))
  plot(range(cs$z), c(-12, 0.8), type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "log density - peak",
    las = 1, bty = "n", xaxs = "i")
  rect(-4, -12, 4, 0.8, col = band, border = NA)
  abline(h = seq(-12, 0, 3), col = grid_col, lwd = 0.8)
  abline(h = -3, lty = 2, col = ink2, lwd = 1.2)
  lr <- log(pmax(cs$ref_d, 1e-300))
  lines(cs$z, lr - max(lr), lwd = 2, col = ink)
  ls <- log(pmax(cs$sn_d, 1e-300))
  lines(cs$z, ls - max(ls), lwd = 2, col = col_sn)
  lines(cs$z, -cs$z^2 / 2, lwd = 1.6, lty = 2, col = col_lap)
  points(cs$zs, cs$scan, pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = muted)
  ends <- c(1, length(cs$zs))
  points(cs$zs[ends], cs$scan[ends], pch = 21, bg = "white", col = ink, cex = 1.4, lwd = 1.5)
  mtext(titles[k], side = 3, line = 1.8, adj = 0, font = 2, cex = 1, col = ink)
  mtext(subs[k], side = 3, line = 0.7, adj = 0, cex = 0.9, col = ink2)
  mtext(
    sprintf("tails: %s (scan end %.1f nats down)",
      if (isTRUE(cs$tails)) "ok" else "heavy", -max(cs$scan[ends])),
    side = 1, line = 2.2, adj = 0, cex = 0.85, col = ink
  )
}
for (k in 1:3) {
  cs <- cases[[k]]
  par(mar = c(5.4, 4, 1, 0.8))
  ymax <- max(cs$ref_d, cs$sn_d) * 1.08
  plot(range(cs$z), c(0, ymax), type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "density",
    las = 1, bty = "n", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  rect(-4, 0, 4, ymax, col = band, border = NA)
  for (out in list(cs$z <= -4, cs$z >= 4)) {
    polygon(c(cs$z[out], rev(cs$z[out])), c(cs$ref_d[out], 0 * cs$z[out]),
      col = fade(ink, 0.18), border = NA)
    polygon(c(cs$z[out], rev(cs$z[out])), c(cs$sn_d[out], 0 * cs$z[out]),
      col = fade(col_sn, 0.55), border = NA)
  }
  lines(cs$z, cs$ref_d, lwd = 2, col = ink)
  lines(cs$z, cs$sn_d, lwd = 2, col = col_sn)
  mtext("posterior SDs from the mode", side = 1, line = 2.1, cex = 0.85, col = ink2)
  mtext(sprintf("outside: exact %s", fmt(cs$ref_out)), side = 1, line = 3.3, adj = 0, cex = 0.85, col = ink)
  mtext(sprintf("scan_end_mass %s", fmt(cs$sem)), side = 1, line = 4.3, adj = 0, cex = 0.85, col = ink)
}
par(op)
```

In the top row, `tails` reads the open circles against the dashed line 3 nats
below the peak. In the bottom row, the orange shading is `scan_end_mass` and
the grey shading is the exact posterior's mass beyond the window.

1. **Well behaved.** The scan ends are about 8 nats down, as for a Gaussian,
   and neither the fit nor the posterior has much mass outside. Both checks
   are rightly quiet.
2. **Heavy inside the window.** A Cauchy posterior is still high at the ends
   of the scan, so `tails` fires, and the fit warns. `scan_end_mass` stays
   under 0.05: the skew-normal has Gaussian tails, so whatever it fits, it
   puts little mass outside the window. It exceeds 0.05 only when the fit
   itself is very wide or very skewed, as for the mixture above.
3. **Heavy beyond the window.** Here the data can only bound a variance from
   above, so its log has a long left tail that only the prior holds back.
   The tail flattens out beyond the window: the scan end is already more than
   3 nats down, and the skew-normal puts little mass outside. Both checks are
   quiet, but the exact posterior has
   `r fmt(cases[[3]]$ref_out)` of its mass outside, against
   `r fmt(cases[[3]]$sem)` for the fit.

The third case is the known limit of a skew-normal at a boundary: no check
that reads only the scanned window can see a tail that starts beyond it.
Jamil and Rue (2026, Section 4.4) find the same miss in the lower tail of a
variance near zero, the boundary pile-up that a unimodal skew-normal cannot
capture. In the structural equation model of the [Rcpp article](rcpp.html),
two log residual variances behave like this, more strongly. Their
skew-normal marginals are too narrow on the log scale, although on the
variance scale the error is much smaller. INLAvaan gives the same marginals
there.

## The warning

The fit-time warning is a condition of class
`inlavanilla_diagnostics_warning`, which is also an `inlavanilla_warning`.
Its headline counts the problems, as INLAvaan's does, and it names at most
three parameters for each; `summary()` lists them all. With `silent = TRUE`
nothing is printed, and every warning raised during the fit is kept in
`fit$warnings` as plain text, which suits simulations:

```{r}
#| label: silent
fit_mix_quiet <- inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2), silent = TRUE)
length(fit_mix_quiet$warnings)
cat(fit_mix_quiet$warnings)
```

To handle the warning in code, catch its class:

```{r}
#| label: catch
fit <- withCallingHandlers(
  inla_vanilla(logpost_mix, c(theta = -0.2)),
  inlavanilla_diagnostics_warning = function(w) {
    message("Check this fit.")
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
```

## Checks on a supplied gradient

When you pass `grad`, it is compared with finite differences of `logpost` at
`init`, per posterior SD, and its Jacobian at the mode is checked for
symmetry, as the Hessian of a function must be. Either failure gives a
warning of its own, because a wrong gradient gives a wrong mode and wrong
marginals.

## References

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026). *Approximate Bayesian inference for structural
equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations*
(arXiv:2603.25690 [stat.ME]). arXiv.
<https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690>
